why: The gateway is the one piece of an AI deployment an FDE can change on a Tuesday without asking the customer's platform team for anything: it is where you swap models, cap spend, survive a provider outage, and prove a new model is better before you make it everyone's problem. Enterprise customers do not accept 'we upgraded the model and it feels better' - they accept a 10% canary with a written comparison of quality, p95 latency, cost per request and error rate, and a rollback that took one config change. Without a gateway you are hard-coding a vendor SDK into the customer's application, which means every model decision becomes a code deploy, a change-advisory-board ticket, and a three-week delay you will personally own.
prerequisites: Evals as infrastructure (topic 53): a versioned eval set, a judge you have calibrated against human labels, and a CI gate - a canary without a quality metric is just a slower way to ship a regression.
LLM observability (topic 54): per-request traces carrying model, tokens, cost and latency, so 'the canary is worse' can be traced to specific requests rather than argued about.
Observability fundamentals (topic 21): Prometheus histograms, PromQL rate() and histogram_quantile(), Grafana dashboards, and OpenTelemetry span attributes.
SRE fundamentals (topic 20): SLIs, SLOs, error budgets - a canary is an error-budget spend decision and you need to be able to say how much budget it may consume.
LLM-era system design (topic 43): retries, rate limits, latency budgets, streaming and TTFT versus total latency, because a gateway multiplies every one of those concerns.
Kubernetes production ops (topic 8) and Redis (topic 31): the gateway runs as a horizontally scaled Deployment whose routing state (cooldowns, TPM/RPM counters) lives in Redis, not in process memory.

subtopics.name: What a gateway must own, and what it must not
subtopics.learn: A model gateway is a seam: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/responses`) in front of N providers, so the application never imports a vendor SDK and never learns a model id. Get clear on what belongs at the seam - credential custody, model aliasing, routing, retries, fallbacks, rate limits, budgets, cost attribution, logging and canary allocation - and what does not: prompt construction, retrieval, business retries, and anything requiring request-body semantics the gateway would have to parse and reinterpret. Know the cost you are accepting in exchange: one more network hop (measure it, LiteLLM exposes `x-litellm-overhead-duration-ms`), one more thing that can be down, and a shared blast radius across every team using it. Run `litellm --config config.yaml` locally and point an unmodified `openai` client at `base_url="http://0.0.0.0:4000"` to feel why the seam is the whole point.

subtopics.name: config.yaml anatomy and the alias indirection
subtopics.learn: Learn the four blocks and what each governs: `model_list` (deployments, each with `model_name` as the client-facing alias, `litellm_params` for the real upstream model/api_base/api_key, and `model_info` for `id`, `mode` and metadata), `router_settings` (routing strategy, fallbacks, cooldowns), `litellm_settings` (callbacks, caching, global defaults) and `general_settings` (master key, database, health-check behaviour). The single most important idea: many `model_list` entries can share one `model_name`, and that is simultaneously how you load-balance, how you fail over and how you canary - one alias, several deployments. Keep secrets out of YAML with `os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` references, pin a stable `model_info.id` per deployment so metrics and headers stay comparable across restarts, and treat config.yaml as code in the customer's repo with review and a diff, never as something edited in the admin UI.

subtopics.name: Routing strategies and where the state lives
subtopics.learn: Know the strategies by behaviour, not by name: `simple-shuffle` (the default and the production recommendation - weighted pick using per-deployment `weight`, or `rpm`/`tpm` as implicit weights, with effectively zero routing overhead), `usage-based-routing-v2` (async, picks the deployment with TPM/RPM headroom), `latency-based-routing`, `least-busy`, and `cost-based-routing`. The trap that catches everyone: routing state - cooldowns, in-flight counts, TPM/RPM windows - is per-process, so with `--num_workers 4` behind three pods you have twelve independent opinions unless you configure Redis, at which point a Redis stall becomes a routing stall. Understand that latency- and usage-based strategies add a read to the hot path and can oscillate (everyone stampedes the deployment that just looked fast), which is exactly why the docs recommend weighted shuffle in production. Set weights explicitly rather than relying on implicit rpm-derived weights, because that is the knob a canary turns.

subtopics.name: Timeouts, retries and cooldowns as one budget
subtopics.learn: Set `router_settings.timeout` globally and override per deployment with `litellm_params.timeout` (cap on the complete response) and `stream_timeout` (cap on time-to-first-chunk - the one that catches a provider that accepts your connection and then sits there). Understand the multiplication: `num_retries` x `timeout` x fallback chain length is your true worst-case latency, and if the caller's own client timeout is shorter than that product you will burn provider spend on responses nobody will ever read. Know `allowed_fails` and `cooldown_time` - after N failures a deployment is pulled from the pool for a cooldown window, which is why a single bad Azure region degrades gracefully instead of taking the alias down. Add `keepalive_seconds` on slow-first-token deployments so an intermediate load balancer does not kill an idle-looking SSE stream (it emits `: ping` comment frames), and remember it is operator-only unless `allow_client_keepalive_override: true` is set.

subtopics.name: The three fallback types and their different meanings
subtopics.learn: LiteLLM splits failover into `fallbacks` (everything else - rate limits, 5xx, timeouts), `context_window_fallbacks` (for `ContextWindowExceededError`, i.e. route to a longer-context model) and `content_policy_fallbacks` (for `ContentPolicyViolationError`, i.e. route to a differently-filtered provider), plus `default_fallbacks` for a misconfigured group. They are applied in list order, so `["model-b", "model-c"]` means b then c, and each hop costs another full timeout. The design questions matter more than the syntax: is a cheaper/weaker fallback model actually acceptable for this workload, or is a 503 better than a quietly worse answer? Does the fallback support the same tool schema, JSON mode and system-prompt semantics, or will the retry fail differently? And is a content-policy fallback a compliance decision the customer's legal team must sign off on rather than an engineering default? Note that `mock_testing_fallbacks` is stripped on the proxy path from v1.85.0 - to test proxy fallbacks you point a deployment at a deliberately broken api_base and send a real request.

subtopics.name: Exception mapping: normalising provider errors
subtopics.learn: The gateway's quiet superpower is turning every provider's idiosyncratic failure into one taxonomy - `RateLimitError`, `ContextWindowExceededError`, `ContentPolicyViolationError`, `AuthenticationError`, `ServiceUnavailableError`, `Timeout`, `APIConnectionError` - because fallback rules, retry policy and alerting all key off that classification. Learn which errors are retryable at all: a 429 with a `retry-after` is, a 400 for a malformed tool schema is not, and retrying it just multiplies the failure. Know that misclassification is a real production bug - a provider that returns a 500 for an over-length prompt will be retried three times and then failed over instead of being routed to a long-context model - so verify the mapping for the specific providers in the customer's stack rather than assuming. Wire the normalised class into your alerts (`exception_class` and `exception_status` are Prometheus labels) so 'the gateway is erroring' becomes 'Bedrock us-east-1 is throttling'.

subtopics.name: Response headers as the attribution spine
subtopics.learn: You cannot analyse a canary you cannot attribute, and the headers are how attribution leaves the gateway. Learn them cold: `x-litellm-model-group` (the alias the client asked for), `x-litellm-model-id` (which deployment row actually answered - this is your canary arm label), `x-litellm-call-id` (join key into logs and traces), `x-litellm-attempted-retries` and `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks` (a request that fell back is not a clean sample and must be excluded or bucketed separately), `x-litellm-response-cost` plus its input/output/cache-read/cache-creation components, and `x-litellm-response-duration-ms` versus `x-litellm-overhead-duration-ms` to separate your hop from the provider's. Note the sharp edge: the response body's `model` field is often restamped to the client-facing alias, so parsing the body to find out which model answered gives you the wrong answer - read the header. Provider headers are passed through prefixed `llm_provider-`, which is where you find real rate-limit remaining counts.

subtopics.name: Tag-based routing as a canary allocator
subtopics.learn: Weights give you a random 10%; tags give you a chosen 10%, which is usually what a customer actually wants ('canary internal users first, never the regulated tenant'). Set `router_settings.enable_tag_filtering: true`, put `tags: ["canary"]` on the candidate deployment and `tags: ["default"]` on the incumbent so untagged traffic has a home, then send `metadata.tags` in the body or the `x-litellm-tags` header. Learn the full grammar because it is how you express real customer constraints: plain tags are OR, `&` prefix means required (AND), `!` prefix is a denylist that removes exactly-matching deployments (`!provider:anthropic` for a tenant with a vendor restriction), and matching is exact string comparison with no regex. Know the failure mode by name: if negation removes every candidate the request fails with `no_deployments_with_tag_routing`, and a banned primary group falls through to the configured `fallbacks` chain - which can silently send your 'never Anthropic' tenant to Anthropic if the fallback is untagged.

subtopics.name: Deterministic bucketing and sticky assignment
subtopics.learn: Per-request randomness is wrong for anything stateful: a conversation whose turn 1 came from model A and turn 3 from model B produces incoherent output and an uninterpretable comparison. Implement assignment as `bucket = crc32(salt + unit_id) % 1000`, where `unit_id` is the session, conversation or tenant - not the request - and `salt` is the experiment name so two concurrent canaries do not correlate their populations. Emit the arm as an explicit tag and as a span attribute so every downstream log, eval and trace carries it, and make the bucketing function a pure, unit-tested function with a test asserting the same unit_id always lands in the same arm and that allocation is within a point of the target across 100k synthetic ids. Decide the exclusion list up front - opt-out tenants, anything under a contractual model commitment, anything in a compliance scope - and enforce it as a denylist tag before bucketing rather than as a downstream filter.

subtopics.name: Canary design: population, dose, duration, blast radius
subtopics.learn: Write the canary plan before touching config: which population (internal, then low-risk tenants, then general), what percentage and for how long, which metrics decide, what the abort thresholds are, and who can press the button. Understand exposure as dose x duration - 10% for 24 hours and 100% for 2.4 hours expose comparable request counts but wildly different blast radius, and only one of them lets a slow-burning failure surface. Plan the ramp explicitly (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with a bake time per step long enough to cover at least one full traffic cycle, because an AI canary started at 09:00 on Monday sees a completely different prompt mix than the same canary at 03:00. Know the two canary-specific traps: a canary that is too small never reaches statistical power on a quality metric with high variance, and a canary that runs too long normalises an unresolved decision into permanent dual-model production.

subtopics.name: The Prometheus surface you actually need for a canary
subtopics.learn: Enable `litellm_settings.callbacks: ["prometheus"]` and scrape `/metrics`; with multiple workers you must set `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR` or your counters are per-worker fiction, and `--prometheus_metrics_port 4001` moves scrape rendering off the inference path. Know the specific series a canary report is built from: `litellm_deployment_success_responses` and `litellm_deployment_failure_responses` (split by `model_id`, so per-arm error rate), `litellm_request_total_latency_metric` (end-to-end histogram in seconds), `litellm_llm_api_time_to_first_token_metric` (streaming only - the number users actually feel), `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric` versus `litellm_overhead_latency_metric` to prove the gateway is not the problem, `litellm_deployment_cooled_down`, `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` / `litellm_deployment_failed_fallbacks`, and `litellm_spend_metric` for cost per arm. Watch label cardinality: `end_user`, `client_ip`, `hashed_api_key` and `user_agent` on high-traffic metrics will melt a small Prometheus, so use `prometheus_exclude_labels` deliberately.

subtopics.name: Histograms and quantiles without lying to yourself
subtopics.learn: Compute quantiles the correct way - `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, model_id) (rate(litellm_request_total_latency_metric_bucket[5m])))` - and understand exactly why you can never average or take the max of two arms' p95s: quantiles are not linear and aggregating them is arithmetically meaningless. Know that a classic histogram quantile is an interpolation within a bucket, so its accuracy is capped by the bucket boundaries: if your buckets top out at 10s and the candidate model routinely takes 25s, its p99 will read as +Inf-adjacent garbage and you will conclude nothing. Always report p50, p95 and p99 together plus the request count per arm, because a p95 computed from 40 canary requests is noise wearing a decimal point. For LLM traffic specifically, separate TTFT from total latency and normalise by output tokens (`litellm_deployment_latency_per_output_token`), otherwise a more verbose model looks slower when it is merely wordier.

subtopics.name: Measuring quality on the canary slice, not in a notebook
subtopics.learn: Latency and error rate are the easy half; the reason model canaries are hard is that the regression is usually in output quality and it is invisible to the gateway. Build three layers: your offline eval set run against both arms as a gate before the canary starts, online proxy signals during it (refusal rate, JSON-parse failure rate, tool-call schema validity, empty-response rate, retry rate, output-token distribution shift - all cheap, all computable without a judge), and a sampled LLM-as-judge pass over paired production requests. Prefer paired comparison where possible: replay the same canary-arm prompts through the incumbent offline and judge A/B with position randomised, which removes population variance and needs far fewer samples than comparing two independent traffic slices. Route all of this through the tracing backend from topic 54 keyed on `x-litellm-call-id` and the arm tag, and capture explicit user feedback (thumbs, edits, regenerate clicks) as the one signal a customer executive will actually believe.

subtopics.name: Enough statistics to defend the promote decision
subtopics.learn: Decide the minimum detectable effect and the sample size before you start, not after you look. For a rate metric (error rate, refusal rate, judge win rate) use a two-proportion test and know roughly what you can detect: distinguishing 2% from 3% at 80% power needs thousands of requests per arm, which tells you immediately whether a 10% canary for one day is even capable of answering the question. Understand the peeking problem - repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon p-value inflates the false-positive rate badly - so either fix the horizon in advance, or use a sequential/always-valid method, or state honestly that the canary is a guardrail rather than an experiment. Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, never bare p-values, and pre-register the decision rule ('promote if judge win rate CI lower bound > 0.45 and p95 regression < 15% and error rate not worse by >0.5pp') so the promote conversation is arithmetic rather than advocacy.

subtopics.name: Automated analysis and one-action rollback
subtopics.learn: A canary a human has to watch is a canary that runs unattended at 3am. Study the Argo Rollouts model even if you implement it yourself: an `AnalysisTemplate` with metric providers (Prometheus queries), a `successCondition` expression, `interval`, `count`, `failureLimit` and `inconclusiveLimit`, attached to canary `steps` with `setWeight` and `pause` so a failing metric aborts and reverts the weight automatically. Map that onto the gateway: a controller that queries per-`model_id` error rate and p95 every 60s and rewrites `weight` in config, or the simpler and more honest version - a documented one-command rollback (`weight: 0` on the candidate, reload) with the exact command in the runbook, tested at least once before the canary goes live. Distinguish abort thresholds (hard, automatic, no discussion: error rate > 2x baseline, p95 > 2x, any content-policy or auth failure spike) from investigate thresholds, and make rollback strictly faster than diagnosis.

resource.label: Argo Rollouts docs - Analysis and progressive delivery

subtopics.name: Spend attribution and budget guardrails during the canary
subtopics.learn: A model canary is a spend experiment as much as a quality one, and 'the new model is 3x the price' is the finding that most often kills a promotion. Turn on cost tracking with a database configured, verify per-request cost lands in `x-litellm-response-cost` and `litellm_spend_metric` broken down by `model_id`, and set `custom_pricing` for any self-hosted or enterprise-contract model where LiteLLM's public price map would be wrong by an order of magnitude. Report cost per successful request rather than cost per token, because a model that is cheaper per token but retries more, thinks longer or produces more output tokens is not cheaper. Put a hard budget on the canary itself - a virtual key or team with `max_budget` and a reset interval scoped to the experiment - so a runaway loop against a premium model is capped by policy rather than discovered on the customer's monthly invoice.

subtopics.name: Running the gateway as production infrastructure
subtopics.learn: The moment the gateway is in front of everything it is the highest-blast-radius component you introduced, so treat it accordingly. Wire `GET /health/liveliness` and `GET /health/readiness` as the Kubernetes probes (readiness returns 503 when the configured database is unreachable, which correctly pulls the pod), and keep `GET /health` - which issues real billed requests to every model - off the probe path; use `background_health_checks: true` with `health_check_interval` instead. Know the production checklist items that bite: run multiple workers and multiple replicas with Redis for shared routing state, do not put the spend database on the request critical path in a way that a slow write stalls inference, set `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR`, disable verbose request logging (customer prompts are PII), and pin the LiteLLM image to a digest because routing behaviour changes between minor versions. Finally, write down what the application does when the gateway itself is down - a direct-to-provider break-glass path is a legitimate design, and 'we never thought about it' is not.

outcomes: You can stand up a LiteLLM proxy in front of at least three providers where one `model_name` alias resolves to multiple deployments, and point an unmodified `openai` Python client at it with no application code change beyond `base_url`.

You can send 10% of traffic to a candidate model using a deterministic, session-sticky bucketing function plus tag routing, and prove from `x-litellm-model-id` on 10,000 requests that the realised split is within one percentage point of the target.

You can write the PromQL that produces a per-arm comparison table - request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, p95 TTFT, fallback count and cost per successful request - each series broken down by `model_id`, and explain why averaging two arms' p95 values is meaningless.

You can demonstrate three distinct failover behaviours on demand by breaking a deployment: `fallbacks` on a 429, `context_window_fallbacks` on an over-length prompt, and `content_policy_fallbacks` on a refusal, each visible as a `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` increment.

You can state, before starting a canary, the minimum detectable effect your traffic volume supports for the chosen quality metric, and say honestly when the canary is a guardrail rather than an experiment.
You can roll back a canary to 0% in under two minutes with a single documented command, and show a rehearsal timestamp proving you have executed that command before the canary went live.

You can produce a written canary report that ends in an explicit PROMOTE / HOLD / ROLLBACK recommendation with pre-registered thresholds, and defend the cost-per-successful-request figure to a customer who only cares about the invoice.

You can explain and mitigate the gateway's own failure modes: shared routing state in Redis, health probes that do not bill you, PII-safe logging, image pinning, and a documented break-glass path when the gateway itself is unavailable.
failureModes: Routing state lives in per-process memory because Redis was never configured, so with four workers across three pods a deployment that should be in cooldown keeps receiving traffic from eleven other processes and the 'failover' never actually fails over.

The canary is assigned per request instead of per session, so a single conversation alternates between two models mid-thread, the output style flips between turns, and the customer reports the product as broken rather than as being tested.

A tenant with a contractual restriction is excluded from the candidate model with a `!provider:x` tag, but the fallback chain is untagged, so the first 429 on their primary silently routes their data to exactly the provider the contract forbids.

Latency histogram buckets were sized for the incumbent model and top out at 10 seconds; the reasoning-model candidate routinely takes 25 seconds, so its p95 reads as an artefact, the dashboard looks fine, and the regression is discovered by users.

The canary decision is made by watching the dashboard and calling it when the numbers look good, which is peeking at a fixed-horizon test - the team promotes on noise and the 'improvement' evaporates at 100%.

`num_retries: 3` with a 120-second timeout and a two-deep fallback chain produces a worst-case of over ten minutes, so during a provider brownout the gateway's connection pool fills with requests whose callers timed out minutes ago and the whole endpoint stops serving healthy traffic.

Cost is compared per token instead of per successful request, so the 'cheaper' candidate ships and the next invoice is 40% higher because it retries more, emits more output tokens, and gets no prompt-cache hits since its cached prefix differs.
interviewQuestions: A customer wants to move from GPT-class to Claude-class models across a live support product with 200k requests a day. Design the rollout end to end: allocation mechanism, what you measure, how long you run it, your abort criteria, and what you tell their VP of Engineering at each stage.

Your canary shows the candidate model is 4% better on judge win rate and 30% slower at p95. How do you decide? Walk me through what additional data you would pull and what you would need to know about the product before you had an opinion.

Explain the difference between load balancing, failover and canarying when all three are implemented by putting multiple deployments behind one model alias. Where do they conflict, and how do you keep a canary's traffic share from being distorted by cooldowns and retries?

Traffic to your gateway is 5% errors and the customer says 'the AI is down'. You have Prometheus and the gateway's response headers. Give me your first five minutes: what you query, what each result would rule in or out, and where you look for the difference between a provider outage, a gateway saturation problem and a bad config push.

Design a fallback policy for a healthcare intake workflow where a wrong answer is worse than no answer. Which of the three fallback classes do you enable, which do you deliberately leave off, and how do you make that decision auditable for their compliance team?

You have a 10% canary running for 24 hours on a metric that moves from 2% to 3%. Is that a real regression? Show me how you would reason about sample size and how your answer changes if the customer will only give you 1% of traffic.

The gateway is now a single point of failure for every AI feature in the customer's product and their platform team is nervous. Convince them it is the right architecture, then tell them honestly what you would build to survive the gateway itself being down.
proofOfWork: Ship a reusable `canary-kit` against the Kaupex stack: a LiteLLM proxy deployed on the cluster with a single `chat` alias fronting three deployments (incumbent, candidate, and a deliberately hostile fake provider you write as a small FastAPI service with configurable latency, 429 rate, content-policy refusals and over-length errors), a pure `assign_arm(unit_id, salt) -> str` bucketing module with tests asserting stickiness and allocation accuracy over 100k synthetic ids, and a `canary.py` CLI with three verbs - `start --pct 10`, `report`, `rollback` - where `rollback` is timed and its execution time recorded. The report verb queries Prometheus for per-`model_id` request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 total latency, p95 TTFT, fallback and cooldown counts and cost per successful request, joins them to per-request quality signals (JSON validity, refusal rate, tool-schema validity, and a sampled paired LLM-as-judge run with randomised position) keyed on `x-litellm-call-id`, and emits a markdown report with a pre-registered decision rule at the top and a PROMOTE / HOLD / ROLLBACK verdict at the bottom. Include a Grafana dashboard JSON with the arm-split panels, a chaos script that drives the fake provider through each of the three fallback classes and captures the resulting `litellm_deployment_successful_fallbacks` deltas as evidence each path works, and a RUNBOOK.md giving the abort thresholds, the one-command rollback, the break-glass direct-to-provider path, and a short 'what I would tell the customer' section written for a non-engineer.
